contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you wrote a research question. Today: find and evaluate real sources to answer it!

Not all sources are equally trustworthy. Check three things: who wrote it (do they have real expertise?), where it's published (is it a reliable, established outlet?), and when it was published (is the information current, especially for fast-changing topics?). Pick a real or hypothetical source for your Day 1 research question, and evaluate it against all three criteria.
You just evaluated a source using real credibility criteria! Tomorrow we'll learn to take notes without plagiarizing.

objectives: Evaluate a source's credibility using author expertise, publication reliability, and currency
Apply all three criteria to a real or hypothetical source
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's research question.
2. Introduce the three source-evaluation criteria.
3. Have the child evaluate a source against all three.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's note-taking/plagiarism lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a clearly-strong example (a scientist's peer-reviewed article) and a clearly-weak example (an anonymous social media post) to make the criteria concrete first
Ready for more: ask the child to think of a source that might pass one criterion but fail another
This is a genuine real-world skill directly connecting to the course's 'digital citizenship' description too
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is an open-ended evaluation activity — check that the child applies all three criteria (author expertise, publication reliability, currency) sensibly to their chosen source.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 7 Writing standard W.7.8: gathering relevant information from multiple sources, assessing credibility of each source, continuing this week's research-paper thread.

generationData.instructions: Evaluate your source against each criterion.

rows.problem: Does the author have real expertise on this topic?
